key: Ask where the process sits and what the basal cells are doing: BPH is hyperplasia of the transition zone around the urethra with basal cells intact, while adenocarcinoma arises in the peripheral zone and has lost its basal cell layer.
items: Periurethral glands and stroma overgrow here, which is why BPH narrows the urethra early.
Smooth symmetric gland on rectal exam
Diffuse nodular growth enlarges the whole gland evenly without a discrete hard nodule.
Hyperplastic glands keep their two-cell lining, so p63 stains the basal cells.
Glands and stroma both multiply under DHT
5-alpha-reductase type 2 converts testosterone to DHT, which makes glands and stroma multiply together; cancer is a clonal epithelial tumor, although it also needs androgens.
Alpha-1A blockade relaxes smooth muscle tone in the stroma and bladder neck.
Blocking DHT formation reduces the bulk of the adenoma, and PSA falls by about half.
Hyperplasia does not progress to carcinoma; the two diseases are separate processes.
Seventy to eighty percent of cancers begin in the posterior zone against the rectum.
Posterior tumors are palpable as firm, irregular nodules.
Loss of p63-positive basal cells in small crowded glands is the key diagnostic criterion.
Alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase is overexpressed in malignant glands and helps confirm cancer.
Tumor cells wrap around nerves in the prostate, a typical feature of adenocarcinoma.
Spread through the Batson venous plexus causes dense, sclerotic lesions in the spine and pelvis.
Gland architecture, not nuclear atypia, defines the Gleason pattern and the Grade Group.
